title: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
summary: How Linux io_uring replaces readiness plus syscalls with two shared rings: SQEs and CQEs, head and tail math, batching, links, CQ sizing, SQPOLL, fixed resources and multishot networking.
outcomes: Explain why epoll plus read and Linux AIO both cost a syscall per I/O, and how a completion model removes it
Compute ring slots and pending counts from free-running head and tail counters, including wraparound
Write correct submit and reap logic, matching CQEs by user_data and keeping buffers alive until completion
Choose between links, drains and app-side waiting, and size the CQ so completions never overflow
Decide when SQPOLL, IOPOLL, registered resources and multishot with provided buffers are worth their cost

lessons.title: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O

blocks.md:
Recall the epoll event loop: `epoll_wait` tells you *which* file descriptors are ready, and then you call `read` or `recv` on each one yourself. This is a **readiness** model. The kernel answers "can this be done now without blocking?" and your program still performs every transfer with its own system call.

Two costs fall out of that. First, a wakeup that reports 50 ready sockets turns into 51 system calls. Second, readiness only exists for things like sockets and pipes. `epoll_ctl` refuses regular files with `EPERM` ([epoll_ctl(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/epoll_ctl.2.html)), because a disk read is never "ready" in advance: it may simply have to wait for the device.

So programs that read files asynchronously used private thread pools: hand the blocking `pread` to a worker, wait for the answer. Linux also had a native async interface, **Linux AIO** (`io_setup`, `io_submit`, `io_getevents`). Jens Axboe's io_uring paper lists why it never became the general answer:

- It is only asynchronous for `O_DIRECT` (unbuffered) I/O. Normal buffered I/O behaves synchronously.
- Even then submission can block, for example waiting for file metadata or for a free request slot on the device.
- Each I/O copies 64 + 8 bytes at submission and 32 bytes at completion (104 bytes) and needs at least two system calls: one to submit, one to reap.

blocks.title: Reading 3 ready sockets: epoll versus io_uring

scenes.caption: The epoll program asks which descriptors are ready. The kernel answers with 3 ready sockets but no data yet.
Now it must fetch the data: one read per socket, each a separate trip into the kernel. That is 4 system calls for 3 transfers.
The io_uring program first writes 3 receive requests into memory it shares with the kernel. Writing to shared memory is not a system call.
One io_uring_enter both submits the 3 requests and waits for 3 results. The kernel writes the results into the shared completion ring, where the app reads them directly.

blocks.md: epoll is a **readiness** API: it tells you when an operation *could* succeed, then you do it. io_uring is a **completion** API: you describe the operation (read these bytes into this buffer), and the kernel tells you when it is *done* and what it returned.

blocks.title: System calls per wakeup as the batch grows

scenes.caption: 1 ready socket: epoll_wait plus one read is 2 system calls; io_uring needs 1 io_uring_enter. SQPOLL (lesson 5) lets a kernel thread pick up requests, so it can need 0. Simplified: one batch, data already there.
8 ready sockets per wakeup: epoll needs 1 epoll_wait plus 8 read calls = 9; io_uring submits 8 receives and waits in 1 io_uring_enter; an awake SQPOLL thread with a busy-polled CQ needs 0.
64 ready sockets per wakeup: epoll needs 1 epoll_wait plus 64 read calls = 65; io_uring submits 64 receives and waits in 1 io_uring_enter; an awake SQPOLL thread with a busy-polled CQ needs 0.

blocks.prompt: A thread-pool server serves buffered file reads. Most requested blocks are already in the page cache. What does each cached read cost in the thread-pool design?
blocks.reveal:
Still a round trip through another thread. The application cannot know whether a block is cached (asking needs more system calls and the answer is racy), so it must bounce **every** request to a worker: at least two context switches even when the data was in memory all along.

The io_uring paper calls this out: io_uring first tries the operation inline, so a cached read completes during the submit call itself and its completion is already waiting when `io_uring_enter` returns.

blocks.md: io_uring, merged in Linux 5.1 (May 2019), was designed around these complaints. Axboe's stated goals were no memory copies for submissions or completions, no shared locks between the application and the kernel, and one interface for files, sockets and more. The solution is a pair of **single-producer, single-consumer ring buffers** in memory shared by your process and the kernel. The rest of this course is about how those rings work and what you can build on them.

blocks.question: An epoll-based proxy wakes up and `epoll_wait` reports 50 readable sockets. How many system calls does it take to read all of them, and how many with io_uring if it submits 50 receives and waits for 50 completions in one call?
options: 50 with epoll, 50 with io_uring
51 with epoll, 1 with io_uring
2 with epoll, 2 with io_uring
51 with epoll, 51 with io_uring because each receive still enters the kernel
blocks.explain: epoll needs the `epoll_wait` plus one `read` per socket: 51. With io_uring the 50 requests are plain memory writes into the submission ring, and a single `io_uring_enter` submits them and waits for 50 completions. The receives still run in the kernel, but they no longer each need their own system call.

blocks.question: Why could a server not just add its data files to epoll to get asynchronous buffered file reads?
options: epoll only supports up to 1024 descriptors
epoll works for files but only with O_DIRECT
epoll reports files as ready but read() on them returns EAGAIN
Regular files are not pollable: epoll_ctl rejects them, and a file read can block on the disk however ready the descriptor looks
blocks.explain: Readiness has no meaning for a regular file, and `epoll_ctl` returns `EPERM` for one. A read that misses the page cache must wait for the device, so the only pre-io_uring options were a thread pool or Linux AIO with its `O_DIRECT` restriction.

lessons.title: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail

blocks.md: `io_uring_setup(entries, &params)` creates an instance and returns a file descriptor for it. The application then `mmap`s three regions through that descriptor: the **submission queue (SQ) ring**, the **completion queue (CQ) ring**, and the array of **submission queue entries (SQEs)**. On kernels that report `IORING_FEAT_SINGLE_MMAP` the two rings share one mapping, so two `mmap` calls suffice. The `params` struct comes back filled with the real ring sizes and the offsets of each field inside the mappings.

A **SQE** is a 64-byte request: an `opcode` (such as `IORING_OP_READ`), `flags`, the `fd`, a file offset `off`, a buffer `addr` and `len`, and a 64-bit `user_data` tag. A **CQE** (completion queue event) is 16 bytes: the same `user_data` copied back untouched, a result `res`, and `flags`.

`res` is what the equivalent system call would have returned: the byte count for a read, or **minus the errno** on failure (a read that fails with `EIO` gives `res = -EIO`). `errno` is never used, since nothing synchronous happened.

blocks.caption: Simplified from io_uring(7). The real SQE packs many op-specific fields into unions.

blocks.md:
Each ring has a **head** and a **tail**, and exactly one side writes each. On the SQ, the app produces (writes the tail) and the kernel consumes (writes the head). On the CQ the roles flip. Because each index has a single writer, no lock is needed, only memory ordering.

Head and tail are **free-running 32-bit counters**: they only ever increase and wrap naturally at $2^{32}$. The slot is the counter masked by the ring size, which is why ring sizes are powers of two. Since a full ring and an empty ring are told apart by the counter difference, every slot can be used without a separate "full" flag.

blocks.caption: N is the number of ring entries (a power of two). Unsigned 32-bit subtraction gives the mod for free.

blocks.title: A 4-entry SQ and 8-entry CQ in motion

scenes.caption: Empty rings. SQ has 4 slots (mask 3), CQ has 8 (mask 7, twice the SQ, the default). On both rings head equals tail, which means empty.
The app fills 3 SQEs (reads A, B, C) at slots 0, 1, 2 and only then advances the SQ tail to 3. Nothing has been sent to the kernel yet.
io_uring_enter(to_submit=3): the kernel consumes the 3 SQEs and moves the SQ head to 3. The slots may be reused now, even though the reads are still in flight.
Completions arrive out of order: B, then C, then A, each 4096 bytes. The kernel writes each CQE at the CQ tail and bumps the tail to 3.
The app reads 2 CQEs and stores CQ head = 2. Those 2 slots are now free for the kernel to overwrite. A's CQE at slot 2 is still pending.
3 new SQEs at tail values 3, 4, 5. Masking wraps them to slots 3, 0, 1 (4 & 3 = 0). The counter just keeps growing; only the slot index wraps.

blocks.prompt: An 8-entry CQ has head = 4294967294 and tail = 1 (the tail counter has wrapped past $2^{32}$). How many CQEs are pending, and in which slots?
blocks.reveal: Three. $(1 - 4294967294) \bmod 2^{32} = 3$. The pending counters are 4294967294, 4294967295 and 0, which mask to slots 6, 7 and 0. Plain `unsigned` arithmetic in C gets this right without any special case, which is exactly why the counters are allowed to wrap.

blocks.md: One asymmetry: the CQ ring holds the CQEs directly, but the SQ ring holds **indices into the separate SQE array** (the `array` field). The paper explains this lets applications keep SQEs inside their own data structures and still submit several in one go. Newer kernels offer `IORING_SETUP_NO_SQARRAY`, which drops the indirection and submits SQEs in ring order.

**Memory ordering.** CPUs and compilers may reorder plain stores. Publishing a request is two steps: fill the SQE, then advance the tail. The tail store must be a *release* store so that every SQE field is visible before the new tail is. The kernel *acquire*-loads the tail before reading SQEs. On the CQ side the app acquire-loads the CQ tail before reading CQEs, and release-stores the head after it is done with them.

blocks.title: One read through the raw rings

scenes.caption: Read our own tail (6) and mask it with 3 (a 4-entry SQ). 6 & 3 = 2, so this request goes in slot 2.
Fill the SQE: a 4096-byte read at offset 0, tagged with user_data 42 so we can recognise its completion later.
Put the slot number in the SQ index array, then publish with a release store of tail 7. Release ordering guarantees the kernel sees the whole SQE before it sees the new tail.
One system call: submit 1 SQE and wait for at least 1 completion (IORING_ENTER_GETEVENTS).
Acquire-load the CQ tail. Our head is 10, the tail is now 11, so one CQE is waiting at slot 10 & 7 = 2 (8-entry CQ).
The CQE carries back user_data 42 and res 4096 (bytes read). Releasing head 11 hands the slot back to the kernel.

blocks.md: If the tail update becomes visible before the SQE fields, the kernel can read a half-written request (say, the right opcode with a stale fd). This is a real bug class in hand-rolled ring code. liburing does the barriers for you, which is the main reason to use it even if you want raw control elsewhere.

blocks.question: A 4-entry SQ has tail counter 9. Which slot does the next SQE go into?
options: Slot 1, because 9 & 3 = 1
Slot 9, the tail value
Slot 0, because the ring is full after 4
Slot 2, because the next SQE goes one past the tail: 10 & 3 = 2
blocks.explain: The slot is `tail & (entries - 1)` = 9 & 3 = 1. The tail counter itself is never reset; it just keeps counting and the mask wraps it onto the 4 slots.

blocks.question: A hand-written submit path does: `*sq_tail = tail + 1;` then fills `sqe->fd`, `sqe->addr` and `sqe->len`, then calls `io_uring_enter`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since io_uring_enter is what actually submits
The tail must be decremented, not incremented
The kernel may read the SQE as soon as the tail moves (an SQPOLL thread can do so at any moment), so it can see stale fields; fill first, then release-store the tail
user_data must be set before fd
blocks.explain: The tail is the publication point. Once it moves, the SQE belongs to the kernel, and with SQPOLL a kernel thread may consume it without waiting for any system call. Always fill the SQE completely and then advance the tail with release semantics.

lessons.title: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request

blocks.md:
The system call that drives everything is `io_uring_enter(fd, to_submit, min_complete, flags, sig)`. `to_submit` says how many new SQEs to consume. With `IORING_ENTER_GETEVENTS` in `flags`, the call also waits until at least `min_complete` CQEs are available. One call can therefore submit a batch **and** wait for results.

The return value is the number of SQEs consumed. Errors belonging to an individual request (bad fd, I/O error) are not returned by the syscall: they arrive as a CQE whose `res` is negative.

Almost nobody writes the barrier code by hand. **liburing**, Axboe's helper library, wraps setup (`io_uring_queue_init`), SQE preparation (`io_uring_get_sqe` plus `io_uring_prep_*` helpers), submission (`io_uring_submit`, `io_uring_submit_and_wait`) and completion handling (`io_uring_wait_cqe`, `io_uring_peek_cqe`, `io_uring_cqe_seen`).

blocks.title: Three reads with liburing

scenes.caption: liburing's io_uring_queue_init does io_uring_setup plus all the mmap work. Asking for 8 entries gives an 8-entry SQ and, by default, a 16-entry CQ.
Grab a free SQE, prepare a 4096-byte read at offset 0, tag it with user_data 0. Nothing has entered the kernel.
Same for blocks 1 and 2 (offsets 4096 and 8192). Three SQEs now sit in the SQ, still invisible until submit advances the tail.
io_uring_submit_and_wait publishes the tail and makes one io_uring_enter call: submit 3, wait for 3. It returns the number of SQEs submitted.
Walk the CQEs. They come back in completion order, not submission order: here block 2 finished first. user_data is how we tell them apart.
scenes.output:
req 2 res 4096
req 0 res 4096
req 1 res 4096

scenes.caption: Advance the CQ head by 3 in one store, returning all three slots to the kernel, then tear the ring down.
scenes.output:
req 2 res 4096
req 0 res 4096
req 1 res 4096

blocks.md: Completions can arrive in **any order**. The ring preserves the order in which requests are *attempted*, not the order in which they *finish*. Always identify a CQE by its `user_data` (often a pointer to your per-request state), never by its position.

blocks.title: System calls per I/O versus batch size

scenes.caption: Readiness model: each batch costs one epoll_wait plus one read per request, so the cost per I/O never drops below 1 system call.
Completion model with submit-and-wait: one io_uring_enter per batch, so the cost per I/O is 1/batch. At 8 requests it is 0.125. Simplified: assumes all results arrive within the wait.

blocks.md: **How a request executes.** Submission does not hand every request to a thread. The kernel first tries the operation inline in non-blocking mode. If it would block, a pollable file (socket, pipe) gets an internal poll registration and the operation retries when the file is ready; other work runs asynchronously, for example on io_uring's own worker threads. That inline-first design is why cached buffered reads cost no more than a plain `read`.

blocks.title: What the kernel does with one SQE

scenes.caption: Every request is first attempted inline, without blocking, inside the submitting call.
Fast path: a read whose data is in the page cache, or a recv on a socket that already has bytes, completes right there. The CQE is waiting before io_uring_enter returns.
Socket with no data yet: instead of parking a thread, io_uring arms an internal poll (IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL) and retries the recv when data arrives. This is epoll's readiness, used inside the kernel.

Work that cannot be polled and would block is executed asynchronously, for example on io_uring's kernel worker threads. IOSQE_ASYNC skips the inline attempt. Simplified: storage I/O can also complete from the device's own completion path.

blocks.md: **Lifetimes.** Once the kernel has consumed an SQE, its slot can be reused immediately: the kernel keeps a private copy of anything it still needs. That is not true of the memory the SQE *points to*. A read's destination buffer, or a write's source buffer, is used while the operation is in flight and must stay valid until its CQE arrives. With SQPOLL, io_uring(7) says every pointer you pass must stay valid until completion.

A classic bug: `char buf[4096];` on the stack of a function that preps a read, submits, and returns. The kernel later writes 4096 bytes into a stack frame that now belongs to someone else. Buffers belong to the kernel from submission until the matching CQE.

blocks.question: A helper function declares `char buf[4096]` locally, prepares an `IORING_OP_READ` into it, calls `io_uring_submit`, and returns. The caller later waits for the CQE. What happens?
options: Safe: the kernel copied the SQE at submit time, buffer included
The submit fails with -EFAULT because stack buffers are rejected
Safe as long as the read hits the page cache
Undefined behaviour: the read may complete after the function returned and write into a dead stack frame
blocks.explain: The kernel copies the SQE, not the buffer it points to. If the read does not complete inline it finishes later and writes into memory that may now hold another function's locals. Even the page-cache case is not guaranteed to complete inline. Keep buffers alive until their CQE arrives.

blocks.question: `io_uring_enter(fd, 4, 4, IORING_ENTER_GETEVENTS, NULL)` returns 4, but one of the four reads used a closed file descriptor. Where does the application learn about it?
options: In the CQE for that request, which has res = -EBADF
io_uring_enter returns -1 with errno = EBADF
Nowhere: invalid requests are silently dropped
io_uring_enter returns 3 instead of 4
blocks.explain: Per-request errors travel in the CQE's `res` as a negative errno. The syscall return only covers how many SQEs were consumed and errors not tied to a single request.

lessons.title: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows

blocks.md:
By default SQEs are independent: the kernel may run them in parallel and they finish in any order. That is what makes io_uring fast, but some work has dependencies. The textbook case is data integrity: write some blocks, then `fsync`, and the `fsync` must not start before the writes are done.

io_uring offers two tools, set in the SQE `flags` field.

- `IOSQE_IO_DRAIN`: this SQE does not start until **every previously submitted** SQE has completed, and later SQEs do not start until it completes. Simple, but it is a barrier for the whole ring.
- `IOSQE_IO_LINK`: the **next** SQE does not start until this one completes successfully. A chain runs from the first linked SQE to the first one without the flag. Chains run independently of other SQEs and of each other, and they do not span separate submissions.
- If a linked request fails, the rest of the chain is completed with `-ECANCELED`. A **short** read or write counts as failure. `IOSQE_IO_HARDLINK` keeps the chain going regardless of the result.

blocks.title: Two writes and an fsync, four ways

scenes.caption: No flags: all four requests start together. The fsync may finish before write B has even reached the file, so it does not cover B. Illustrative timings.
IOSQE_IO_LINK on A and B: A then B then fsync run as one chain. Correct, but A and B are now serialized. Reads X and Y are outside the chain and run freely.
IOSQE_IO_DRAIN on the fsync: it waits for everything submitted before it (including unrelated read X), and read Y, submitted after, waits for the fsync. A full pipeline barrier.
A broken chain: write B comes back short (fewer bytes than asked). io_uring treats that as failure, so the linked fsync never runs and completes with -ECANCELED.

blocks.prompt: You link a 4096-byte `IORING_OP_READ` to an `IORING_OP_WRITE` that copies the same buffer to another file. The read hits end-of-file and returns 1000. What does the write's CQE say?
blocks.reveal: `res = -ECANCELED`. io_uring considers any unexpected result an error, and a read that returned fewer bytes than requested breaks the chain, so the linked write never runs. A copy loop must handle short reads itself, or use `IOSQE_IO_HARDLINK` and check each result.

blocks.md: **Timeouts and cancellation.** `IORING_OP_TIMEOUT` completes after a time or after a given number of other completions, waking any waiter. `IORING_OP_LINK_TIMEOUT`, linked after a request, cancels that request if it is still running when the timer fires (the timeout's CQE then reads `-ETIME`). `IORING_OP_ASYNC_CANCEL` cancels an in-flight request by its `user_data`; socket I/O is usually cancellable, disk I/O that has already started usually is not.

**Flow control.** The SQ size limits how many requests you can hand over **in one batch**, not how many can be in flight: once the kernel consumes an SQE the slot is free again. Every in-flight request still needs room for its CQE, though. liburing's default CQ is twice the SQ, which suits storage but may be too small for network servers.

If completions arrive with the CQ full, kernels with `IORING_FEAT_NODROP` keep the extra CQEs on an internal overflow list and set `IORING_SQ_CQ_OVERFLOW`. That avoids losing events, but it is a slow path, and `io_uring_enter` can return `-EBUSY` if it cannot flush the backlog.

scenes.caption: SQ has 32 entries, so the default CQ has 64. The app submitted in batches of up to 32 and now has 100 receives in flight. The SQ size never limited that.
A burst: all 100 complete before the app looks. 64 CQEs fill the ring; with IORING_FEAT_NODROP the other 36 go to an internal overflow list and IORING_SQ_CQ_OVERFLOW is set.

The app reaps 64; the kernel then flushes the 36 overflowed CQEs into the freed slots. Nothing was lost, but the overflow path is slower, and io_uring_enter may return -EBUSY until the backlog is flushed.
The fix is sizing: with IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE and cq_entries = 256, the whole burst of 100 fits in the ring and overflow never happens.

blocks.md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

blocks.question: Your app writes 4 blocks then needs an fsync, while unrelated reads stream through the same ring. Which option keeps the 4 writes parallel and never stalls the unrelated reads?
options: Set IOSQE_IO_DRAIN on the fsync
Link write 1 to write 2 to write 3 to write 4 to fsync with IOSQE_IO_LINK
Submit the 4 writes, wait for their 4 CQEs, then submit the fsync (or use a separate ring for integrity writes)
Set IOSQE_ASYNC on the fsync
blocks.explain: A drain stalls everything else in the ring, and a link chain serializes the writes. Waiting for the 4 write CQEs before submitting the fsync keeps the writes parallel and leaves the other traffic alone. The paper also suggests a separate ring for integrity writes if drains are frequent.

blocks.question: A ring was created with 64 SQ entries (so 128 CQ entries). Can the application have 500 operations in flight?
options: No, the SQ size is a hard limit on in-flight requests
Yes, the SQ only limits batch size, but it must size the CQ (or reap fast enough) for 500 completions or it hits the slow overflow path
Yes, and the CQ size does not matter because CQEs are never dropped
No, io_uring_enter returns -EINVAL above 128 in flight
blocks.explain: Consumed SQE slots are reused immediately, so in-flight count is not capped by the SQ. The real constraint is CQ space: overflowed completions go to a slow kernel list, and `-EBUSY` can appear while it drains.

lessons.title: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs

blocks.md:
Once the system-call cost is gone, per-request kernel overheads show up. Two opt-in features remove them, both set up with `io_uring_register(2)`:

- **Registered files.** Every request with a plain fd makes the kernel take and drop an atomic reference to the file. `IORING_REGISTER_FILES` registers an fd array once; requests then set `IOSQE_FIXED_FILE` and put the array **index** in `sqe->fd`.
- **Registered buffers.** For `O_DIRECT` I/O the kernel must map your pages for each request and unmap them afterwards. `IORING_REGISTER_BUFFERS` maps a set of buffers once; `IORING_OP_READ_FIXED` and `IORING_OP_WRITE_FIXED` then do I/O within them, picked by `buf_index`.

Two setup flags trade CPU for latency:

- `IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL` busy-polls the storage device for completions instead of waiting for an interrupt. It needs `O_DIRECT` files and a device configured for polling (for NVMe, the driver's `poll_queues` parameter), and you reap completions by calling `io_uring_enter`, since nothing arrives on its own.
- `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` starts a kernel thread that polls the SQ, so submissions need no system call while it is awake. `sq_thread_idle` (milliseconds) sets how long it spins before sleeping; the paper gives one second as the default. Early kernels required privileges for SQPOLL; recent ones do not.

blocks.title: SQPOLL: submission without a system call

scenes.caption: With IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL a kernel thread watches the SQ tail. The app writes an SQE and release-stores the tail: an ordinary memory write.
The poll thread notices the new tail, consumes the SQE and issues the I/O. When it completes, the CQE lands in the shared CQ, where the app can see it by reading memory.
After sq_thread_idle milliseconds with nothing to do, the thread goes to sleep and sets IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP in the SQ ring flags.
Now a tail store alone is not enough. The app must check the flag after publishing and call io_uring_enter with IORING_ENTER_SQ_WAKEUP. liburing's io_uring_submit does this check for you.

blocks.md: SQPOLL is not a free "go faster" switch. The poll thread consumes a CPU while it spins. io_uring_sqpoll(7) warns it can hurt low-IOPS, bursty or CPU-bound workloads and that it only speeds up submission, not completion handling. Benchmark with and without it.

**Networking needs two more ideas.** A completion-based `recv` names its buffer at submission time, so 100,000 idle connections would pin 100,000 buffers. **Provided buffer rings** fix this: the app registers a pool (a buffer group), sets `IOSQE_BUFFER_SELECT`, and the kernel picks a buffer only when data actually arrives, reporting its id in the CQE.

**Multishot** requests post many CQEs from one SQE. One multishot accept yields a CQE per new connection; one multishot recv yields a CQE per arrival. `IORING_CQE_F_MORE` on a CQE means the request is still armed; a CQE without it means it ended (error, cancel, or buffers exhausted) and must be resubmitted.

blocks.title: Multishot recv drawing from a provided buffer ring

scenes.caption: The app registers a 4-entry buffer ring (buffer group 1) holding buffers b0 to b3, and submits one multishot recv per connection with IOSQE_BUFFER_SELECT. No buffer is tied to any connection yet.
Data arrives on connection 7. Only now does the kernel pick a buffer (b0). The CQE has res = bytes, IORING_CQE_F_BUFFER with buffer id 0 in the upper 16 bits of flags, and IORING_CQE_F_MORE.
Connection 9 then connection 7 again: b1 and b2 are consumed, one CQE each. Still a single SQE per connection, because F_MORE means the recv stays armed.
The app finishes with b0's data and adds b0 back to the ring. Ownership of a buffer passes to the kernel when added and back to the app when its CQE is posted.

Two more arrivals take b3 and b0. Then connection 9 gets data with the ring empty: its recv fails with -ENOBUFS and that CQE has no F_MORE, so the multishot recv has ended and must be re-armed after replenishing.
From Axboe's paper: Linux AIO hit a cliff at 608K IOPS on his test box, while io_uring drove about 1.2M without polling, roughly twice as much.

With IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL (busy-polling the NVMe device instead of waiting for interrupts) io_uring reached about 1.7M. AIO cannot poll, so this part is not like for like. One 2019 machine: read the ratios, not the absolute numbers.

blocks.md:
**Tradeoffs and failure modes.**

- *Ordering on streams.* io_uring(7) warns against more than one outstanding send, or more than one outstanding recv, on the same TCP socket unless you use links or the multishot and bundle features, since the kernel may reorder them.
- *Complexity.* Buffer lifetimes, CQ sizing and re-arming multishot requests are your problem now.
- *Security surface.* Google reported in 2023 that 60% of submissions to its kCTF kernel exploit program targeted io_uring, and in response disabled it on ChromeOS and made it unreachable to Android apps. Linux has the `io_uring_disabled` sysctl, which can turn io_uring creation off entirely or limit it to privileged processes and a chosen group.

io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

blocks.question: A configuration service does about 50 small reads per second in short bursts, on a 2-core VM that is already busy. A teammate proposes `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` to save system calls. Good idea?
options: Yes, SQPOLL always lowers latency
Yes, but only with IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL as well
No: at 50 I/O per second the syscalls saved are negligible, and the poll thread competes for one of only 2 busy CPUs and keeps going to sleep between bursts
No, because SQPOLL requires root on all kernels
blocks.explain: SQPOLL pays off when a stream of submissions keeps the thread busy. Here it would mostly spin or sleep and wake, costing CPU on a constrained machine for almost no saved work. Privilege is no longer required on recent kernels, so that is not the reason.

blocks.question: A multishot recv posts a CQE with `res = -ENOBUFS` and no `IORING_CQE_F_MORE` flag. What should the server do?
options: Nothing: the recv stays armed and retries automatically
Close the socket, since ENOBUFS means the peer disconnected
Increase the SQ size
Return buffers to the provided buffer ring, then submit a new multishot recv for that socket
blocks.explain: The missing `F_MORE` says the multishot request has terminated, here because the buffer group ran dry. Replenish the ring (the app must keep returning consumed buffers) and re-arm the recv. The connection itself is fine.
